summary.summary: Bedford's 2025/26 Annual Governance Statement reports a £17.7m overspend against a £177.6m net budget, driven mainly by Children's Services (£14.3m overspend, 30% of its budget) and Adult Social Care. Usable reserves stood at just £14.2m at 31 March 2026, and the council states it applied for Exceptional Financial Support explicitly 'to avoid issuing a Section 114 Notice' - receiving £22m for 2025/26 and having £58m approved in principle for 2026/27 (£25m core support plus £33m against a Wixams Station cost risk). The council forecasts a further £27m budget gap in 2027/28 growing to a cumulative £58.6m by 2029/30, even as Adult Services (CQC: 'Requires Improvement') and Children's Services (Ofsted: 'Requires Improvement to Good') both remain under external improvement scrutiny. Despite this, the Head of Audit's overall opinion on the governance and control framework is 'Reasonable'.

signals.headline: Bedford applied to MHCLG for £20m plus £2m (Cleat Hill) of Exceptional Financial Support for 2025/26 explicitly 'to avoid issuing a Section 114 Notice'; approved in principle February 2026.
signals.why: The council is on record stating a statutory insolvency notice was the alternative to receiving EFS - a direct distress marker.

signals.headline: EFS received: £22m for 2025/26 (£20m core + £2m Cleat Hill); £58m approved in principle for 2026/27 (£25m core + £33m for the Wixams Station cost risk).
signals.why: Two consecutive years of Exceptional Financial Support, with the 2026/27 figure more than double the prior year, shows the underlying budget gap widening rather than closing.

signals.headline: Usable reserves were £14.2m at 31 March 2026, described as a 'diminishing level' that triggered a CIPFA Resilience Review; the council aims to rebuild reserves to within a recommended risk-assessed range by 31 March 2027.
signals.why: Thin reserves leave little buffer against further in-year overspends, particularly given ongoing demand pressures in social care.

compliance.notes: Strong, comprehensive strategy: exemplary liability benchmark (charted to 2051/52 and used to shape the borrow-vs-redeem-pooled-funds decision), full asset-life MRP policy statement, robust creditworthiness policy (CDS beyond ratings), integrated ESG policy, and a clear gross-debt-below-CFR multi-year indicator. Weakest areas: the core interest-rate exposure requirement (RISK-02) - no fixed/variable exposure indicator with an upper limit despite the text referring to one; several commercial/non-treasury disclosures only partial (paras 51-53 compliance statement, income-dependence contingency, quantified proportionality/limits); and missing sterling-only borrowing and audit-qualification statements. Note the Council holds investment property (GBP86.5m, GBP3.6m net income) held partly for financial return, so commercial-investor requirements were scored as applicable even though it reports no Prudential-Code 'commercial investments'.

news_drafts.headline: Bedford forecasts needing £23.629m exceptional support at year-end after contingencies, against a £25.000m line
news_drafts.lead:
Bedford Borough Council forecasts that it would need £23.629m of exceptional financial support at the end of the year, once contingencies are used, against a £25.000m line for that support. Exceptional financial support is permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending. The figure is in the budget monitoring report to the Budget and Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee, which meets on 3 December. The paper says "the amount of EFS required would be £23.629 million following the use of contingencies as shown in the table below".

The calculation starts from the £25.000m support line and adds the £4.206m the council forecasts it will overspend. It then takes off four amounts held against that position: a £2.000m general contingency, a £1.439m contingency for efficiencies not achieved, a £0.500m transport turbulence reserve and a £1.638m social care turbulence reserve.

The paper lists a further £1.000m Energy Resilience Reserve separately. The council holds it, and the calculation does not apply it. The committee has the table and the forecast in front of it at the 3 December meeting.

news_drafts.headline: Bedford's 2026/27 budget rests on £25m of exceptional financial support, with up to £10m assumed for 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Bedford's 2026/27 budget, approved on 18 February 2026, is supported by £25m of exceptional financial support, the government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The council's medium-term financial strategy, before Full Council on 25 November, says the budget would not be possible without it and that a section 114 notice, the formal declaration that a council cannot balance its budget, would otherwise be necessary. Bedford is one of 37 councils receiving such support for 2026/27.

The strategy's forecast does not include any further support, and assumes the £25m received in 2025/26 is not carried forward. It carries a planning assumption of up to £10m of exceptional financial support in 2027/28, which the paper says is consistent with discussions with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. That figure is excluded from the estimates in the report. The paper says support is limited to 2027/28, as the council indicated to the ministry in December 2025.

The budget strategy sets out that the council must move to a financially sustainable position not reliant on exceptional financial support "as soon as possible, whilst recognising demand and inflationary pressures are likely to increase". The paper links this aim to the council's Improvement Plan and to the resilience review carried out by the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy.

news_drafts.headline: Bedford Schools' Forum told high needs deficit forecast at £7.175m for 2026/27, against £4.482m budgeted
news_drafts.lead:
Bedford Borough Council's high needs deficit for 2026/27 is forecast at £7.175m, up from the £4.482m budgeted, the Schools' Forum was told on 23 November. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. Forecast spending is £41.471m against a budget of £38.778m, a variance of £2.693m. The paper gives the cause as top-up costs and other alternative provision.

The high needs reserve is forecast to move from a deficit of £3.692m at 1 April 2026 to £10.867m at 31 March 2027. The government's Department for Education confirmed on 27 October a High Needs Stability Grant of £1.510m for the council, which the paper says is 90% of the dedicated schools grant deficit at 31 March 2026. The paper says the department will continue to take an appropriate and proportionate approach to deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28, but that support will not be unlimited. The council will need to meet the residual deficit from its schools grant budget in 2028/29, with reserves set aside in the preceding years; the paper gives no figure for it.

An appendix puts the net overspend across the grant at £7.014m, with underspends of £0.040m on central school services and £0.121m on early years. It records an approved transfer of £1.470m from the Schools Block to high needs for targeted special educational needs. The paper lists eight actions to address the high needs deficit and gives no savings figure for any of them. It also gives a forecast deficit of £7.344m in its resource implications section, without explaining the difference from £7.175m.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: External audit fees are forecast £235k under budget, from revised estimates for current and previous years.
findings.detail: The paper says the underspend is partly offset by staffing pressures in Council Tax collection within Resources, so the net effect across the organisation is neutral.
findings.matters: Audit fee estimates for previous years being revised down is a signal a finance director would check against their own audit cost position.
findings.quote: The forecast underspend is arising from revised estimates for the audit fees relating to current and previous years.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Bereavement income mitigation has reduced the originally forecast shortfall by £125k.
findings.detail: The paper says the bereavement income plan is already having a positive impact and that the Environment directorate is at a £201k underspend overall, despite pressures on Highways, Planning and the coroner service.
findings.matters: Recovery of a forecast income shortfall through a named plan is a specific result other councils facing similar income pressure can compare against.
findings.quote: with bereavement income increasing and reducing the originally forecast shortfall by £125k.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Adult Services forecasts a £979k underspend at October, moved from £835k at September.
findings.detail: The paper says the forecast underspend moved in a positive direction in the period, supported by transformation, direct payments and care package reviews. It also notes that the position depends on demand and growth assumptions for the remaining five months.
findings.matters: An overspend recovered in a demand-led service is an uncommon result that finance directors elsewhere would want to see the drivers for.
findings.quote: Period 7 for Oct is showing a forecast underspend of £979k

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: The transformation savings line carries a £1.500m shortfall against targets not yet distributed to service budgets.
findings.detail: The paper says the shortfall sits in the Financing budgets pending distribution to service budgets, and that a fortuitous underspend from the 3.3% pay award will partly mitigate the Whole Organisation Restructure shortfall.
findings.matters: A savings target held centrally that has not been allocated to services is a clear way to see how much of the savings plan is not yet attached to a budget line.
findings.quote: There is a shortfall on various savings targets not yet distributed to the relevant service budgets.

findings.committee: Budget and Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: The sundry debt collection rate at October is 94.50% of debt raised, with £124.485m collected from £131.729m raised.
findings.detail: The paper says the council had been collecting over 100% of debt raised before October. It reports £8.930m of invoices under 30 days old that are not yet due. Adult Services debt is about £12m, and an enforcement agent contract has been re-tendered with three awards.
findings.matters: The collection rate and the age of the debt show how quickly the council is turning billed income into cash, which is a key indicator for lenders.
findings.figures: 94.50% collection rate; £124.485m collected; £131.729m raised; £8.930m under 30 days; about £12m Adult Services debt; 25.00% arrears target over 91 days
findings.quote: representing a collection rate of 94.50% of debt raised.
